Original heading

The vision of the Scriptures of truth.

Persian and Greek rulers, and their conflicts (verses 1–30)

The angel showed Daniel the succession of the Persian and Greek empires.

The kings of Egypt and Syria were also described.

Judea lay between their territories and suffered because of their conflicts.

Henry notes that verses 5–30 are generally understood as describing events under those governments.

He also says that from verse 21 onward, the prophecy is generally understood as referring to Antiochus Epiphanes, a cruel and violent persecutor of the Jews.

Consider how quickly worldly splendor, wealth and the power used to obtain them decay and disappear.

In his Providence, God raises one ruler and removes another as he chooses.

This world is filled with wars and conflicts arising from human desires.

God foresees perfectly every change of government, revolution and event.

Not one word he has spoken will fail.

His purposes and declarations will certainly come to pass.

While the rulers of this world fight one another like potsherds of the earth, they sometimes win and sometimes lose, deceive others and are themselves deceived.

But those who know God will trust him.

He will enable them to stand firm, carry their cross and endure their conflict.

Later conflicts and the final hope (verses 31–45)

Henry calls this remaining part of the prophecy very difficult.

He notes that commentators disagree considerably about its meaning.

He suggests that the account may pass from Antiochus to antichrist.

He sees possible references to the Roman Empire, the fourth monarchy, in its pagan, early Christian and papal forms.

These remain Henry's tentative historical-prophetic identifications, not explicitly named entities in the prophecy.

The end of God's anger toward his people approaches, as does the end of his patience toward his enemies.

To escape the ruin awaiting unbelief, idolatry, superstition, cruelty and open ungodliness, let us make God's word our standard for truth and conduct, the foundation of hope and the light along our path.

It will guide us through this dark world toward the glorious inheritance above.
classic_reading:
[Dan.11.1-Dan.11.30]
Chapter 11
The vision of the Scriptures of truth.
Verses 1-30 The angel shows Daniel the succession of the Persian and Grecian empires. The kings of Egypt and Syria are noticed: Judea was between their dominions, and affected by their contests. From [Dan.11.5-Dan.11.30] Dn 11:5-30, is generally considered to relate to the events which came to pass during the continuance of these governments; and from [Dan.11.21] Dn 11:21, to relate to Antiochus Epiphanes, who was a cruel and violent persecutor of the Jews. See what decaying, perishing things worldly pomp and possessions are, and the power by which they are gotten. God, in his providence, sets up one, and pulls down another, as he pleases. This world is full of wars and fightings, which come from men's lusts. All changes and revolutions of states and kingdoms, and every event, are plainly and perfectly foreseen by God. No word of God shall fall to the ground; but what he has designed, what he has declared, shall infallibly come to pass. While the potsherds of the earth strive with each other, they prevail and are prevailed against, deceive and are deceived; but those who know God will trust in him, and he will enable them to stand their ground, bear their cross, and maintain their conflict.
[Dan.11.31-Dan.11.45]
Verses 31-45 The remainder of this prophecy is very difficult, and commentators differ much respecting it. From Antiochus the account seems to pass to antichrist. Reference seems to be made to the Roman empire, the fourth monarchy, in its pagan, early Christian, and papal states. The end of the Lord's anger against his people approaches, as well as the end of his patience towards his enemies. If we would escape the ruin of the infidel, the idolater, the superstitious and cruel persecutor, as well as that of the profane, let us make the oracles of God our standard of truth and of duty, the foundation of our hope, and the light of our paths through this dark world, to the glorious inheritance above.

The resurrection and final deliverance (verses 1–4)

The name Michael means “Who is like God?”

Henry understands this name and the title “the great Prince” as pointing toward the divine Savior, Christ.

Christ stood in place of his people as their sacrifice.

He bore the curse that they deserved to remove it from them.

He now stands for them as their Intercessor at the throne of grace.

After the destruction of antichrist, Henry expects the Lord Jesus to appear upon earth at the last day and bring about the complete redemption of his people.

When God delivers his people from persecution, the change is like life from the dead.

As the gospel spreads, people who seem asleep in dust are awakened to spiritual life.

Henry speaks of this awakening among Jews and Gentiles.

At the end, the multitude sleeping in the dust will literally awaken.

Some will rise to life, others to shame.

Future glory is reserved for all God's saints, those who are wise concerning their souls and eternity.

Those who help turn many people toward righteousness—bringing sinners back from error and helping save their souls from death (James 5:20)—will share the joy and glory of those they helped reach heaven.

That joy will increase their own happiness.

The remaining prophetic times and Daniel's hope (verses 5–13)

One angel asked how long these extraordinary events would last.

The reply was “a time, times, and half a time,” the period also mentioned in Daniel 7:25 and Revelation.

Henry interprets this as 1,260 prophetic days, or years, beginning when the power of God's people was scattered.

He suggests that what he calls “the imposture of Mohammed”, referring polemically to Islam, and papal domination began at roughly the same period and represented a twofold attack upon the church.

These are Henry's polemical chronology and historical identification, not a firm date supplied by the biblical passage.

Despite the long conflict, everything will end well.

Every power opposing God's purpose will be overthrown.

Holiness and love will triumph and be honored forever.

This prophecy encompasses many different events over successive ages, reaching even to the general resurrection.

Daniel was encouraged by the prospect of his own happiness at death, at judgment and through eternity.

It is good for all of us to consider our departure from this world.

We must leave it, but not until God calls us and has completed the work he assigned to us here.

It is as though God then says: Go your way. Your work is finished. Others may take your place.

The comfort Daniel received belongs to every faithful believer.

Whatever their circumstances during life, they will receive a good portion at the end.

This should be everyone's chief concern.

With such hope we can be content with our present circumstances and welcome God's will.

Believers can know happiness already: they rest in God by faith now, and a fuller rest is reserved for them in heaven.
classic_reading:
[Dan.12.1-Dan.12.4]
Chapter 12
The conclusion of the vision of the Scriptures of truth. ( [Dan.12.1-Dan.12.4] Dn 12:1-4) The times of the continuance of these events. ( [Dan.12.5-Dan.12.13] Dn 12:5-13)
Verses 1-4 . Michael signifies, "Who is like God," and his name, with the title of "the great Prince," points out the Divine Saviour. Christ stood for the children of our people in their stead as a sacrifice, bore the curse for them, to bear it from them. He stands for them in pleading for them at the throne of grace. And after the destruction of antichrist, the Lord Jesus shall stand at the latter day upon the earth; and He shall appear for the complete redemption of all his people. When God works deliverance from persecution for them, it is as life from the dead. When his gospel is preached, many who sleep in the dust, both Jews and Gentiles, shall be awakened by it out of their heathenism of Judaism. And in the end the multitude that sleep in the dust shall awake; many shall arise to life, and many to shame. There is glory reserved for all the saints in the future state, for all that are wise, wise for their souls and eternity. Those who turn many to righteousness, who turn sinners from the errors of their ways, and help to save their souls from death, James 5:20, will share in the glory of those they have helped to heaven, which will add to their own glory.
[Dan.12.5-Dan.12.13]
Verses 5-13 One of the angels asking how long it should be to the end of these wonders, a solemn reply is made, that it would be for a time, times, and a half, the period mentioned [Dan.7.25] Dn 7:25, and in the Revelation. It signifies 1260 prophetic days or years, beginning from the time when the power of the holy people should be scattered. The imposture of Mohammed, and the papal usurpation, began about the same time; and these were a twofold attack upon the church of God. But all will end well at last. All opposing rule, principality, and power, shall be put down, and holiness and love will triumph, and be in honour, to eternity. The end, this end, shall come. What an amazing prophecy is this, of so many varied events, and extending through so many successive ages, even to the general resurrection! Daniel must comfort himself with the pleasing prospect of his own happiness in death, in judgment, and to eternity. It is good for us all to think much of going away from this world. That must be our way; but it is our comfort that we shall not go till God calls us to another world, and till he has done with us in this world; till he says, Go thou thy way, thou hast done thy work, therefore now, go thy way, and leave it to others to take thy place. It was a comfort to Daniel, and is a comfort to all the saints, that whatever their lot is in the days of their lives, they shall have a happy lot in the end of the days. And it ought to be the great care and concern of every one of us to secure this. Then we may well be content with our present lot, and welcome the will of God. Believers are happy at all times; they rest in God by faith now, and a rest is reserved for them in heaven at last.
